definition.text: The laws and agencies that limit pollution and reduce its harm, together with the measurement of pollution levels.

facts.text: Locally, regulation is usually overseen by environmental agencies or the public health system.
The modern regulatory system began with US rules on industrial and mining air and water pollution in the 1960s and 1970s.
Because many pollutants cross borders, UN treaties regulate them, such as the Montreal Protocol on ozone-depleting chemicals in 1987.
Polluters have historically lobbied governments of poorer countries to keep regulation lax.

title: Pollution prevention
article: Regulation and monitoring of pollution#Pollution prevention

definition.text: A strategy of cutting the amount of waste created in the first place, rather than treating it after release, especially by industry, farms and consumers.

facts.text: Many large corporations see it as a way to make production more efficient and profitable through less waste and better technology.
In the US it was written into law through the Pollution Prevention Act of 1990 and the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments.

title: Regulatory economics

definition.text: The study and use of government rules to achieve economic aims, such as correcting market failures and protecting the environment.

facts.text: Regulation is law imposed by government on people and private firms to change economic behaviour; some industries instead regulate themselves.
Government agencies are always at risk of regulatory capture by the industries they regulate.
Principal-agent theory treats the government as principal and the regulated operator as agent, to deal with the operator knowing more than the regulator.
Supporters argue regulation guards against monopoly, instability and environmental harm, drawing on thinkers such as Karl Polanyi.
Economists such as Milton Friedman, George Stigler and Friedrich Hayek argue for limiting government's role in markets.
Regulatory intervention can counter a market failure, so some economists think some regulation beats an unregulated market.

contested_note: Economists disagree sharply on whether regulation generally improves or worsens market outcomes.
distinct_from: Positive and normative theories of regulation

title: Positive and normative theories of regulation

definition.text: Two families of theory: positive theories explain why regulation happens, normative theories say how regulators should act.

facts.text: Positive theories say regulation arises to overcome information gaps, protect customers from market power, protect operators from rivals or from government opportunism.
Normative theories say regulators should reduce information costs, set efficient prices and run independent, transparent and predictable processes.

definition.text: A rule requiring electricity suppliers to get a set share of their power from renewable sources such as wind, solar, biomass and geothermal.

facts.text: Certified renewable generators earn certificates for each unit of electricity, sell them to suppliers, who hand them to the regulator to prove compliance.
Supporters say relying on the market brings competition and innovation that deliver renewable energy at the lowest cost.
RPS-type schemes exist in the UK, Italy, Poland, Sweden, Belgium and Chile and in 29 of 50 US states.
A US national laboratory credits state standards with 60% of the rise in US renewable electricity since 2000, though their share of new builds is falling.
Like subsidies, renewable portfolio standards create protected markets for renewable energy, an alternative to feed-in tariffs.
